section_summary: This section documents mounting American public, religious, press, and congressional pressure during May–July 1939 to halt exports of arms, scrap iron, petroleum, and other strategic materials to Japan during its war in China. State Department replies explain the limits of the Neutrality Act, report that licensed arms shipments to Japan had effectively ceased, and distinguish those controlled articles from unrestricted commodities. The section also contains Chinese criticism of American trade with Japan, polling data favoring a boycott and embargo, proposed legislation, and extensive lists of organizations protesting assistance to Japan.

subfiles.title: Arthur Capper requests additional copies of the Department's statement on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Capper asks for twenty-five more copies of a State Department statement concerning exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Capper thanks Hull for his May 22 letter and considers its explanation suitable for constituents troubled by arms and war-supply shipments to Japan. He notes that he receives daily letters from Kansas and requests additional mimeographed copies for public use.

subfiles.title: Reply supplying Capper with twenty-five copies of the export statement
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Capper's request and encloses twenty-five copies of the Department's China–Japan export statement.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply acknowledges Capper's May 23 letter. It forwards twenty-five copies of the mimeographed State Department statement on exports of war materials to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Philip Smead Bird's protest against supplying Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a letter protesting U.S. supplies to Japan and enclosing a church resolution.
subfiles.summary: The file note points to another decimal-file location for the original correspondence. It describes a protest against supplying Japan with war materials and a resolution adopted by the Church of the Covenant on May 12, 1939.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to World Peace Foundation statement on an embargo against treaty violators
subfiles.about: The sheet references a World Peace Foundation statement favoring embargoes against Japan or other violators of the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference summarizes an opinion adopted by the trustees of the World Peace Foundation on May 10. It concerns U.S. neutrality legislation and embargoes on exports to, or imports from, Japan or any other violator of the Nine-Power Treaty.

subfiles.title: George A. Dondero forwards a Farmington petition against shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Dondero forwards a petition from Farmington residents and asks for the Department's position on shipments supporting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Representative Dondero reports receiving a petition opposing goods shipments that help Japan maintain its war against China. He encloses the petition and requests a statement of the State Department's current attitude.

subfiles.title: Farmington citizens' petition for a boycott of war-supporting shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Farmington residents ask Dondero to support an immediate boycott of goods or materials sustaining Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that the United States can no longer morally sanction support for the destruction of China. Its signers request a boycott of all goods and materials contributing to Japan's war until the conflict ends.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Dondero on exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Hull provides the Department's export statement and explains its policy against supplying aircraft used to bomb civilians.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges the Farmington petition and sends copies of the Department's statement for Dondero and the petitioners. He recalls the July 1938 moral embargo on aircraft and aeronautical supplies for countries bombing civilians. He adds that no new Japanese arms-export licenses had been sought or issued for five months and expects remaining shipments under older licenses soon to cease.

subfiles.title: D. Lane Powers forwards a petition on traffic in war materials with Japan
subfiles.about: Powers forwards a petition concerning trade in war materials with Japan for State Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: Representative Powers encloses a petition received that day relating to the traffic in war materials with Japan. He asks the Secretary of State to give it attention.

subfiles.title: File note describing the petition forwarded by Powers
subfiles.about: The note records that Powers's enclosure was a form petition signed by organizations and individuals.
subfiles.summary: The file note characterizes the missing enclosure as a standard-form petition about exports of war materials to Japan. It records that both organizations and individuals signed it.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Powers and returns the petition
subfiles.about: Hull notes the petition, explains the moral embargo and decline in licensed arms exports to Japan, and returns the enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hull assures Powers that the petition's information will receive appropriate consideration and encloses the Department's export statement. He describes compliance with the Department's disapproval of aeronautical supplies to forces bombing civilians. No new Japanese arms licenses had been sought or issued for five months, and the few remaining exports were proceeding under older licenses expected soon to lapse.

subfiles.title: Washington Committee for Aid to China transmits a 6,500-signature petition
subfiles.from: Mortimer Graves, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: The committee submits a petition seeking lawful American action against Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The committee forwards a petition carrying 6,500 signatures and calling for American action against Japanese aggression under existing law. Although legislative circumstances had changed since the petition was circulated, the committee says the signers still want the State Department to lead in defining an honorable and peace-promoting policy.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Typed copy of the Washington Committee's petition letter
subfiles.from: Mortimer Graves, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: This typed copy reproduces the committee's submission of its 6,500-signature petition.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats the committee's appeal for action against Japanese aggression within existing law. It emphasizes that the signatories want the State Department to guide American policy toward the conflict in China and promote peace.

subfiles.title: Roster of Washington Committee for Aid to China sponsors
subfiles.from: Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: The page lists the committee's religious, civic, political, and professional sponsors.
subfiles.summary: The roster identifies thirty-four sponsors associated with the Washington Committee for Aid to China. The names include clergy, politicians, academics, military figures, and civic leaders.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledges the Washington Committee petition
subfiles.about: Hull thanks Graves for the committee's views and returns the petition for possible further use.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Hornbeck brought Graves's letter and petition to his attention and expresses appreciation for the views of the committee and signers. The Department has noted their contents and returns the petition because the committee may wish to use it again.

subfiles.title: Internal note recording Welles's refusal to transmit domestic petitions to Congress
subfiles.about: The note records Welles's view that the Department should not serve as a conduit between domestic organizations and Congress.
subfiles.summary: Welles distinguishes Americans in Chengdu, who lacked ready access to Congress, from organizations based in the United States. He strongly opposes having the Department transmit the latter's views to congressional committees and suggests only informing the Secretary.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck routing note requesting consultation with Welles
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks that his recommendation about the Washington Committee petition be discussed with Welles.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes that extra copies of the relevant letter have been prepared and attached. He directs staff to consult Welles about the recommendation on the third page of his memorandum.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on the Washington Committee petition
subfiles.about: Hornbeck reports receiving the committee's petition and recommends notifying congressional foreign-relations chairmen.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck records that Frederick Brown Harris presented Mortimer Graves's letter and a petition signed by 6,500 people. The petition calls for stopping shipments of oil, scrap iron, cotton, timber, and other materials to Japan, while Harris says the committee supports Hull's policies. Hornbeck explains that foreign policy rests on public opinion but often requires legislative authorization, and he recommends sending copies to the chairmen of the relevant Senate and House committees.

subfiles.title: J. Will Taylor asks about wartime sales to Japan, Germany, and Italy
subfiles.about: Taylor asks whether U.S. manufacturers may sell Japan anything it can buy and whether the same policy applied to Germany and Italy during the Spanish Civil War.
subfiles.summary: Taylor requests clarification concerning current American sales of munitions and munitions materials to Japan. He also asks whether manufacturers were permitted to sell freely to Germany and Italy during the Spanish conflict.

subfiles.title: Department reply explaining export law to Taylor
subfiles.about: Hull explains the cessation of licensed arms shipments to Japan and the legal limits of the 1937 neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the Department's China–Japan export statement and reports that no Japanese arms-export licenses had been issued for six months; earlier licenses had expired or been used. He explains that Germany and Italy were not subject to an arms prohibition during the Spanish conflict because the President made no finding of war involving them. The 1937 act also gave no authority to prohibit commodities beyond the officially enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Lorimer questions American Far Eastern and Cuban policy
subfiles.about: Lorimer criticizes the contradiction between protesting Japanese bombing and supplying Japan, and questions U.S. policy in China and Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Lorimer points to a British freighter carrying American scrap iron to Japan while naval forces monitor the Pacific. She questions protecting investments and trade in China, invokes the Panay incident, and urges withdrawal from imperialism and dollar diplomacy. She also asks why the United States allegedly supports dictatorship in Cuba while condemning dictatorships elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Interdivisional routing sheet for the Lorimer correspondence
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Division of Controls
subfiles.about: The page routes Lorimer's letter among the State Department divisions responsible for its Far Eastern and Cuban questions.
subfiles.summary: This largely administrative sheet bears the heading of the Division of the American Republics and routing annotations. It accompanies the interdivisional consideration of Mrs. Lorimer's inquiries.

subfiles.title: Bonsal memorandum proposing an answer on Cuba
subfiles.about: Bonsal drafts a response denying that the United States supports any particular Cuban regime.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal quotes Lorimer's questions about American support for dictatorship in Cuba. He proposes replying that U.S.–Cuban relations are conducted on the same sovereign basis as relations with other governments, so the United States cannot be said to support a specific Cuban regime.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum proposing an answer to Lorimer
subfiles.about: The memorandum suggests sending Lorimer earlier official documents explaining U.S. Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: The proposed paragraph directs Lorimer to Senate Document No. 131, departmental press statements from 1937, and Hull's March 1938 address. It says those documents provide detailed information about the policy followed in the Far East and protection of American interests in China.

subfiles.title: Haig requests proposed divisional replies to Lorimer's questions
subfiles.from: R. V. Haig, Division of Controls
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Haig asks the responsible divisions to provide suggested answers to Mrs. Lorimer's questions.
subfiles.summary: Haig notes that Lorimer's letter raises matters falling under several divisions. He asks each division to advise whether an answer is appropriate and what reply it recommends.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Lorimer on Japan, China, and Cuba
subfiles.about: Yost provides the Department's positions on arms exports, American interests in China, and relations with Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the export statement and describes the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies for forces bombing civilians. He reports that no new Japanese arms licenses had been issued for five months and that residual shipments under older licenses should soon end. Additional official documents explain policy in China, while the reply rejects the claim that the United States supports a particular Cuban regime.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note summarizing Fuzhou despatch no. 108
subfiles.about: The note flags a Fuzhou newspaper editorial criticizing American responsibility for continuing aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Fuzhou despatch no. 108 of May 23 and its enclosed editorial. It observes that the despatch's final two paragraphs adequately summarize the criticism of the United States.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 108 on a Fuzhou editorial criticizing the United States
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Consulate, Fuzhou
subfiles.about: Rowe transmits a Chinese editorial holding the United States partly responsible for Japanese aggression because of American arms sales.
subfiles.summary: The vice consul forwards the original and translation of Kuang Kuang-mo's May 13 editorial in Nan Fang Jih Pao. The editorial contrasts Roosevelt's protests with continued American sales to Japan and argues that U.S. sympathy has not produced effective action. It concludes that the United States shares responsibility with Japan for crimes committed in China.

subfiles.title: Chinese text of “Crimes for Which the United States Should Share the Responsibility”
subfiles.from: Kuang Kuang-mo, Nan Fang Jih Pao
subfiles.about: The Chinese-language editorial condemns the contradiction between American professions of peace and continued material aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial cites an appeal from Americans in Chongqing for an embargo following Japanese air raids. It argues that American petroleum, metals, cotton, machinery, and other supplies enable Japanese attacks on China and even on American citizens and property. The writer characterizes U.S. policy as self-defeating and morally inconsistent.

subfiles.title: English translation of “Crimes for Which the United States Should Share the Responsibility”
subfiles.from: Kuang Kuang-mo, Nan Fang Jih Pao
subfiles.about: The translation argues that American trade makes the United States complicit in Japanese aggression and air raids in China.
subfiles.summary: The editorial reproduces the Chongqing Americans' demand for an embargo on commodities used by aggressors and says continued trade contradicts friendship, justice, and world peace. It invokes a Paris peace conference and American newspaper criticism to challenge Roosevelt's inaction. Because American-supplied materials are used against China and American lives and property, the writer calls U.S. policy both complicit and suicidal.

subfiles.title: McCormack forwards Higgins's letter on Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: McCormack forwards a constituent's appeal to stop supplying Japan with war materials and credit.
subfiles.summary: Representative McCormack sends Hull a letter from Dudley L. Higgins, Winchendon's town treasurer. He asks that Higgins's views on the Sino-Japanese conflict receive consideration.

subfiles.title: Higgins urges legislation ending American support for Japan
subfiles.about: Higgins asks McCormack to support legislation stopping war materials and credit from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Higgins states that Japan could sustain its war against China only briefly without American war materials and credit. He urges McCormack to use every legitimate means to obtain legislation ending those supplies.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to McCormack and returns Higgins's letter
subfiles.about: Hull reports that licensed arms shipments to Japan have ceased and returns the constituent letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends the Department's export statement for possible transmission to Higgins and recalls the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies. He states that no Japanese arms licenses had been issued during the preceding six months and that all older licenses had expired or been used. Accordingly, no arms, ammunition, or implements of war were then being shipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Polk forwards “A Suicidal American Policy” and urges international coordination
subfiles.about: Polk forwards C. P. Althaus's editorial and urges investigation and cooperation with Britain and France to restrain Japan.
subfiles.summary: Polk describes Althaus as well acquainted with East Asia after fourteen years' residence there and commends the editorial's proposed solution. He also cites a Christian Science Monitor editorial identifying the United States as Japan's chief arms provider. Polk urges the Department to explore a mutual agreement with Britain, France, and other countries to stop Japanese aggression against American property.

subfiles.title: “A Suicidal American Policy”
subfiles.from: C. P. Althaus, The Bethel Journal
subfiles.about: The editorial calls for coordinated American, British, and French economic pressure against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Althaus reviews the confrontation between Britain and Japan, the vulnerability of foreign concessions, and Japanese attacks on American missions in China. He argues that Japan's advance threatens Western trade and institutions and that the United States is furnishing resources Japan may later use against it. The editorial advocates withholding iron ore, tin, copper, and gasoline through coordinated action with Britain and France.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Polk on the Althaus editorial
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the clipping and reports that no arms or implements of war are currently being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Polk for forwarding Althaus's editorial and encloses the Department's export statement. He recounts the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies to forces bombing civilians. No Japanese arms-export licenses had been issued in six months, and all earlier licenses had expired or been used.

subfiles.title: Capper forwards Southern Baptist boycott and scrap-iron appeal
subfiles.about: Capper forwards Una Roberts Lawrence's letter supporting a Japanese-goods boycott and legislation against scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: Capper says Lawrence's letter resembles many protests he has received concerning U.S. policy toward the Sino-Japanese conflict. He asks whether circumstances have changed since Hull last wrote and requests any public statement he can use in answering constituents.

subfiles.title: Southern Baptist young women appeal for an embargo and boycott
subfiles.from: Una Roberts Lawrence and Katherine Roberts
subfiles.about: Southern Baptist delegates urge legislation ending war-material exports to Japan and endorse a consumer boycott.
subfiles.summary: The Kansas delegation at a Southern Baptist young women's camp says one thousand attendees representing 77,143 women support a boycott of Japanese goods. The writers condemn American-made bombs, aircraft, and weapons used in China and ask specifically whether scrap-iron exports can be ended. They also request Capper's support for the Schwellenbach neutrality bill and promise to circulate his reply.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Capper about the Southern Baptist appeal
subfiles.about: Hull says his earlier export statement remains applicable and supplies updated copies for Capper's use.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Lawrence's letter and says the information sent to Capper on May 22 remains valid. He sends additional copies of the Department's statement, with current China export figures inserted in one copy. He notes that updated statistics can be obtained from the Division of Controls and returns Lawrence's letter.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Moffett's inquiry about scrap-iron restrictions
subfiles.from: E. P. Allen, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Allen records an Iron Age editor's inquiry concerning proposed legislation restricting scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: L. W. Moffett asks whether Congress is likely to impose quotas or restrictions on iron and steel scrap exports and mentions a prospective Schwellenbach bill. He also reports that the Japanese ambassador has urged purchasing agents to secure as much scrap as possible before restrictions appear. Moffett is surprised to learn that the 1937 neutrality resolution does not authorize the President to prohibit scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Egbert Smith condemns American material support for Japan
subfiles.about: Smith urges Hull to end American support for Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Smith says American Christians are humiliated by reports that the country is Japan's chief supplier of munitions and other assistance. Citing missionary reports of murders, rapes, and other atrocities, he asks Hull to find a way to end that support despite the acknowledged difficulties.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Egbert Smith
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Smith's protest and refers him to an earlier reply sent to H. Kerr Taylor.
subfiles.summary: Hull assures Smith that his views on the Far Eastern situation will receive careful consideration. For information about current exports to China and Japan, he refers Smith to the Department's July 10 letter to the church's educational secretary, H. Kerr Taylor.

subfiles.title: Hope requests information on neutrality and exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Hope asks for the State Department's position and export figures so he can answer constituents concerned about the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Representative Hope reports receiving letters about the Sino-Japanese conflict and the failure to invoke neutrality provisions. He requests the Department's position and information on American exports of munitions and primary and secondary war materials to both China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Hope on legal controls and Japanese exports
subfiles.about: Hull explains which exports can legally be restricted and reports no Japanese arms licenses during the first half of 1939.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends copies of the Department's statement and explains that existing law controls only arms, ammunition, implements of war, tinplate scrap, and helium. Other commodities remain freely exportable, with statistics available from the Commerce Department. He also notes substantial compliance with the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies and no Japanese arms licenses during the six months ending June 30.

subfiles.title: Price sends Hamilton evidence of American opposition to war-material exports
subfiles.about: Price forwards materials illustrating American public opposition to exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Writing for the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression, Price calls Hamilton's attention to enclosed evidence of prevailing public attitudes. The enclosure concerns exports of American war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Fact sheet on U.S. war-material exports and pending Far Eastern bills
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The sheet quantifies American supplies to Japan and summarizes four proposed measures for restricting trade or credits.
subfiles.summary: The committee claims the United States supplied approximately 56 percent of Japan's imported war materials in 1938, led by petroleum, iron, machinery, copper, aircraft, and automobiles. It summarizes the Pittman and Schwellenbach resolutions and bills introduced by Representatives Eaton and Coffee. The proposals variously invoke the Nine-Power Treaty, authorize trade restrictions, or directly prohibit arms, strategic materials, and credits to Japan.

subfiles.title: Gallup report on support for a boycott and arms embargo against Japan
subfiles.from: George Gallup, American Institute of Public Opinion
subfiles.to: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The reproduced poll reports sharply increased American sympathy for China and majority support for boycotting Japan and embargoing arms.
subfiles.summary: The poll reports that sympathy for China rose from 47 percent in 1937 to 74 percent, while support for a boycott of Japanese goods reached 66 percent. Seventy-two percent favored forbidding arms shipments to Japan, compared with 40 percent favoring a similar ban on shipments to China. Respondents most often explained their position by identifying Japan as the aggressor.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledges Price's public-opinion materials
subfiles.about: Hamilton thanks Price for providing material on exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Price's June 28 letter and the enclosed evidence about exports from the United States to Japan. He expresses appreciation for Price's thoughtfulness in making the material available.

subfiles.title: Price submits Roosevelt a list of organizations protesting aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Price sends Roosevelt a partial list of organizations opposing war-supply sales to Japan and says they represent nearly forty million citizens.
subfiles.summary: Price states that national, regional, and local organizations have protested continued assistance to Japan, usually requesting governmental action. Allowing for overlap, he estimates that the groups represent nearly forty million people. He argues that their actions and the Gallup poll demonstrate a mounting majority against American support for Japan's invasion of China.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Gallup report enclosed with Price's letter to Roosevelt
subfiles.from: George Gallup, American Institute of Public Opinion
subfiles.about: The enclosure reproduces polling data supporting a Japanese-goods boycott and an embargo on arms shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate of the Gallup report shows growing sympathy for China and declining neutrality toward the Asian war. It reports majorities for boycotting Japanese goods and prohibiting arms shipments to Japan, with respondents viewing Japan as the aggressor.

subfiles.title: Partial list of groups protesting aid to Japan or aggressors
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists national, regional, and local religious, labor, civic, educational, peace, and women's organizations opposing aid to Japan or aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: The six-page compilation identifies national denominations, missionary bodies, labor unions, women's organizations, student groups, peace societies, churches, and local civic bodies that adopted protests or embargo resolutions. It supplies membership or representation figures for many entries and spans communities across the United States. The list documents the geographic and institutional breadth of organized sentiment against shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Green acknowledges Price's submission through the White House
subfiles.about: Green acknowledges the list of organizations protesting shipments of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Writing by White House referral and for the Secretary of State, Green confirms receipt of Price's July 14 letter and enclosure. He thanks Price for transmitting the organizational protest list to the President.

subfiles.title: Cable reporting likely British support for a U.S. embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: The cable reports that Britain is interested in Pittman's bill and would likely follow a congressional embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cable says the European situation has forced the British government temporarily to exercise patience toward Japan. It nevertheless reports strong British interest in Senator Pittman's bill and predicts that Britain would follow if Congress enacted an embargo on war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to draft an appropriate reply
subfiles.about: Welles directs Hamilton to prepare a reply to the attached correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary asks Hamilton to have an appropriate answer drafted for Welles's signature. The note serves as the routing instruction for the incoming letter beginning on the following page.

subfiles.title: Incomplete letter thanking Welles for his stand on American policy
subfiles.about: An unidentified writer thanks Welles for the determined stand he has taken concerning American policy.
subfiles.summary: The surviving opening says the writers are deeply grateful for Welles's determined stand. It adds that many citizens are intensely aroused that the United States is helping and loaning assistance, but the letter continues beyond this section.
